prompt.context: Your client is an entrepreneur looking to invest in a new bar. He needs to determine how profitable the business will be, and convince his primary investor — his father — that it will be a viable business.
prompt.question: What areas would you consider and investigate to assess whether this bar is a viable, profitable business?

clarifying_info.q: Is there an expected return on investment?
clarifying_info.a: The client wants to understand what return he can make, but no specific target has been set.

clarifying_info.q: Will the father be actively involved in management?
clarifying_info.a: No, the father will be a passive investor only.

clarifying_info.q: What type of bar is it?
clarifying_info.a: It will be a sports bar.
Sunday–Wednesday: noon to midnight (12pm–12am). Thursday–Saturday: noon to 2am.
Yes, it will have food service.
Chicago. Consider proximity to competitors, real estate agents, where the target customer segment lives, and segmenting by district.

clarifying_info.q: Will the client buy, rent, or lease?

clarifying_info.a: Kitchen: 4 people at $10/hr (flat) when kitchen is open. Bar: 1 bartender at all times at $5/hr (tips-based). Waitstaff: 3 waitresses at all times at $5/hr (tips-based).

framework: Investment & Financing: startup costs (legal, licenses, remodeling, equipment, staff training), lease deposit (first + last + security), cost of capital, expected ROI, NPV, break-even
Revenue Drivers: food revenue (capacity × spend per customer × hours), drink revenue (customers/hr × spend × hours), peak vs. off-peak traffic, product mix (food vs. drinks)
Cost Structure: rent/lease ($10k/mo), labor (kitchen + bar + waitstaff), COGS (food & beverage), utilities, insurance, ongoing licenses
Customer & Marketing: target segment (upscale men 28–40), bar concept (sports bar), marketing channels, loyalty/retention
Location Analysis: Chicago neighborhood selection, proximity to competitors, real estate agent input, where target segment lives, district segmentation
Viability Assessment: monthly profit/loss, break-even analysis, NPV of investment, sensitivity to revenue assumptions

questions.prompt: Calculate total weekly revenue from food and drinks across all operating days.
questions.guidance: Candidate should organize revenue by day-type (Sun–Wed vs. Thu–Sat), then by time block (12pm–8pm vs. 8pm–close), applying the correct customer counts and spend per customer. A chart or table is strongly recommended. Food spend = $15/customer; drink spend = $20/customer.

math.setup: Two day-types × two time blocks each. For each block: food revenue = food_customers/hr × hours × $15; drink revenue = drink_customers/hr × hours × $20. Sun–Wed = 4 days; Thu–Sat = 3 days.
steps: SUN–WED 12pm–8pm (8 hrs): food = 10 cust/hr × 8 hr × $15 = $1,200; drinks = 4 cust/hr × 8 hr × $20 = $640; subtotal = $1,840/day
SUN–WED 8pm–midnight (4 hrs): food = 4 cust/hr × 4 hr × $15 = $240; drinks = 15 cust/hr × 4 hr × $20 = $1,200; subtotal = $1,440/day
THU–SAT 12pm–8pm (8 hrs): food = 15 cust/hr × 8 hr × $15 = $1,800; drinks = 10 cust/hr × 8 hr × $20 = $1,600; subtotal = $3,400/day
THU–SAT 8pm–2am (6 hrs): food = 5 cust/hr × 6 hr × $15 = $450; drinks = 20 cust/hr × 6 hr × $20 = $2,400; subtotal = $2,850/day

questions.guidance: Candidate must track three staff categories across different operating hour windows: kitchen staff (paid $10/hr, 4 people), bartender (1 person at $5/hr), and 3 waitresses at $5/hr. Hours differ by day-type.

math.setup: Staff cost per hour: kitchen = 4 × $10 = $40/hr; bar = 1 × $5 = $5/hr; waitstaff = 3 × $5 = $15/hr. Total hourly staff cost when all present = $60/hr. Sun–Wed: 12 hrs/day × 4 days = 48 hrs. Thu–Sat: 14 hrs/day × 3 days = 42 hrs. Total hours/week = 90 hrs.
steps: Sun–Wed hours: noon to midnight = 12 hrs/day × 4 days = 48 hrs
Thu–Sat hours: noon to 2am = 14 hrs/day × 3 days = 42 hrs

questions.prompt: Assess monthly profitability and whether the business is viable. What other costs must be considered?
questions.guidance: After computing revenue and labor, candidate should subtract lease ($10k/mo) and estimated COGS (typically 25–35% of food/beverage revenue), plus note startup/one-time costs. Should also discuss break-even, NPV, and sensitivity.

math.setup: Use monthly revenue ~$137,000. Subtract: lease $10,000; labor ~$23,220; COGS ~30% of revenue = ~$41,100. Rough monthly profit before other costs.
steps: Gross operating profit ≈ $137,000 – $74,320 = ~$62,680/month (before utilities, insurance, licenses, marketing)
Startup costs (one-time): legal, licenses, remodeling, equipment, staff training, lease deposit (first + last + security = ~$30,000)
math.answer: Rough monthly operating profit ~$62,680 before utilities/insurance/marketing; one-time startup costs ~$30,000+. Business appears profitable if revenue assumptions hold.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the major cost categories the client should plan for when opening this sports bar?

categories.name: Startup / One-Time Costs
ideas: Equipment (kitchen appliances, bar fixtures, TVs, sound system)

categories.name: Fixed Monthly Costs
ideas: Utilities (electricity, gas, water, cable/satellite for sports)

categories.name: Variable / Operating Costs
ideas: COGS: food and beverage inventory (~25–35% of revenue)

recommendation: The sports bar appears financially viable based on estimated monthly revenue of ~$137,000 against total monthly costs (lease + labor + COGS) of ~$74,000, yielding a gross operating profit of roughly $62,000 before utilities, insurance, and marketing.

The client should proceed with detailed site selection in Chicago targeting neighborhoods where the upscale 28–40 male demographic is concentrated, negotiate favorable lease terms, and build a formal financial model including NPV and break-even analysis before committing capital.
risks: Revenue projections rely on assumed customer traffic that may not materialize, especially during off-peak Sun–Wed slots
Chicago sports bar market may be competitive; proximity to rival establishments could suppress traffic
Liquor liability and regulatory compliance add cost and operational complexity
Startup costs and lease deposit create meaningful upfront cash requirement
next_steps: Conduct site analysis in target Chicago districts; speak to local real estate agents
Build full 3-year P&L with sensitivity analysis on revenue (±20%) and COGS assumptions
Obtain quotes for remodeling, equipment, and licensing to refine startup cost estimate
Explore financing options and calculate IRR/NPV to present to the father-investor
